families.t: ink mixing, colour matching, solvent-borne printing, on-press cleaning, manual and automatic off-press cleaning, ventilation, skin and fire control
f: Gravure control sheets cover ink mixing, solvent-borne printing and press cleaning.
Colour matching and ink mixing should minimise vapour and skin exposure.
Solvent-borne gravure printing requires effective ventilation and process control.
On-press cleaning needs both chemical and moving-machinery controls.
Manual off-press cleaning should minimise open solvent use and direct contact.
Automated off-press cleaning can reduce exposure where correctly enclosed and maintained.
Containers, waste and contaminated wipes should be managed to limit vapour and fire risk.
PPE and skin care should supplement engineering and work-practice controls.
families.g: Gravure chemical risk depends on ink and solvent chemistry, mixing and transfer, press enclosure, cleaning method, ventilation, waste handling, ignition control, skin contact and maintenance.

families.s: HSE digital and wide-format inkjet printing chemical-control guidance
families.t: solvent-borne inks, UV-curable inks, wide and grand format equipment, enclosure, extraction, curing, maintenance, skin contact and waste
f: Digital printing control sheets cover wide-format solvent-borne, wide-format UV-curable and grand-format printing.
Solvent-borne inks can create inhalation and fire hazards.
UV-curable inks can create skin and sensitisation risks before full cure.
Printer enclosure and extraction should control vapour and mist release.
Curing equipment should be maintained and operated within its designed controls.
Ink changes, cleaning and maintenance should minimise direct contact and spills.
Contaminated wipes, cartridges and waste should be contained and disposed of safely.
The assessment should reflect printer size, room volume, ink system, print rate and maintenance frequency.
families.g: Digital-printing risk depends on ink system, printer format and enclosure, ventilation and curing, task frequency, skin contact, cleaning, waste, fire controls and maintenance.

families.s: HSE printing chemical-health-surveillance and skin-control guidance
families.t: UV inks, isocyanates, respiratory sensitisers, dermatitis, risk assessment, occupational-health advice, skin checks, records and control review
f: Printing workers may be exposed to UV-curable inks, isocyanates and other respiratory or skin sensitisers.
Health surveillance should be determined by the COSHH risk assessment.
A competent occupational-health professional can advise on programme design.
Respiratory surveillance may be needed for isocyanates and other respiratory sensitisers.
Skin checks can support early detection of dermatitis.
Surveillance results should be handled confidentially and linked to control review.
Workers should be trained to report early respiratory and skin symptoms.
Health surveillance does not replace elimination, substitution, enclosure or ventilation.
families.g: Printing surveillance need depends on chemical hazard, residual exposure, sensitisation potential, worker susceptibility, valid detection methods, control performance, records and follow-up.

families.t: rubber goods, tyres, chemistry, machinery, dust, fume, cancer, interventions, storage, manual handling, transport and workforce participation
f: Rubber manufacturing combines heavy machinery with continuously developing chemical processes.
The industry includes general rubber goods, new tyres, retreading, recovery, imports, distribution and retailing.
HSE guidance covers occupational cancer, dust and fume, safe interventions and equipment issues.
Sector plans should address accidents and ill health together.
Machinery interventions are a recurring serious-injury risk.
Chemical handling and curing processes require COSHH controls.
Storage, manual handling, load security and workplace transport should be included in site arrangements.
Worker participation and industry action plans can support sustained improvement.
families.g: Rubber-industry risk depends on products and chemistry, process machinery, dust and fume, curing, interventions, storage and transport, maintenance, competence and worker involvement.

families.s: HSE rubber-process dust and fume control guidance
families.t: cancer risk, rubber process dust, rubber fume, WELs, weighing, mixing, milling, curing, ventilation, extraction, monitoring and surveillance
f: Health studies identify increased cancer risk in rubber-processing stages that produce rubber dust and fume.
Exposure should be kept as far below applicable workplace exposure limits as reasonably practicable.
Rubber process dust arises during handling, weighing, adding or mixing ingredients with uncured elastomers.
Rubber fume arises during mixing, milling, blending and conversion of rubber compounds.
Individual chemicals such as carbon black, fillers and solvents may have separate exposure limits.
Ventilation and local extraction should match the dust- or fume-generating task.
Exposure measurement should be used where control adequacy is uncertain.
Health surveillance and records should support early detection and sustained control.
families.g: Rubber dust and fume risk depends on compound and additives, task and temperature, dustiness and fume release, enclosure and extraction, exposure duration, monitoring, maintenance and worker susceptibility.
